introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively (that is, with questions taken from each of the three sections).

Each essay must contain:
- An introduction = 5 marks
- A thesis = 7 marks
- An antithesis = 6 marks
- A synthesis = 3 marks
- A conclusion = 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections). Le sujet ne dit pas explicitement « au moins une par section » ; cela est déduit de « imperatively » et du format des autres années. `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Les deux sous-sections de la Section Three (Descartes, texte de philosophie africaine) sont comptées comme une seule section de deux questions ; le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les questions 5 et 6 à la fois.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs propres points par sous-question.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités (Sophistes, Socrate, Kierkegaard, Nkrumah, Nyerere, Gyekye, Wiredu, Mbiti, Césaire, Fanon, Descartes, Hume, Kant...) sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale ni numéro de page ; les dates et faits historiques cités sont donnés dans leurs grandes lignes. À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), code 0790, JUNE 2021, trois heures.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Socrates' philosophy is diametrically opposed to that of the Sophists. Discuss this assertion focusing on their Ethics and Epistemology.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** In fifth-century BC Athens the Sophists (Protagoras, Gorgias, Hippias, Prodicus and, in Plato's portrayal, Thrasymachus) were travelling teachers who charged fees to train young men in rhetoric and political success. Socrates (about 470-399 BC) wrote nothing; he questioned his fellow citizens in the public places of Athens and is known mainly through Plato and Xenophon. To say that his philosophy is "diametrically opposed" to theirs means that on the two questions set, ethics (what is virtue and how should one live?) and epistemology (what can be known, and how?), the two sides hold contrary positions. The problem is whether the opposition is total, or whether the two camps share more than the assertion admits.

**Thesis: Socrates and the Sophists are opposed (7 marks).**

*Epistemology.* The Sophists were relativists or sceptics. Protagoras' saying that man is the measure of all things is usually read as meaning that what appears true to each person is true for that person. Gorgias is reported to have argued that nothing exists, that if anything existed it could not be known, and that if it could be known it could not be communicated. Truth therefore gives way to opinion (doxa) and to persuasion: the best speaker, not the best informed, wins the argument. Socrates, by contrast, believed in knowledge (episteme) that is stable and universal. His questions "What is justice? What is courage?" look for a definition valid in every case, reached by cross-examination (the elenchus) and a dialectic that moves from particular examples to the common essence. His profession of ignorance, as Plato reports it in the Apology, is not scepticism: knowing that one does not know is the first step of inquiry, and it drives the search for real knowledge.

*Ethics.* The Sophists generally taught that moral rules are conventions (nomos) that differ from city to city. Some, such as Thrasymachus in the Republic and Callicles in the Gorgias (as Plato presents them), went further and claimed that justice is the interest of the stronger and that natural right favours the strong. Virtue (arete) meant success and skill in public life, a technique that could be taught for a fee. Socrates held that virtue is knowledge of the good, that no one does wrong willingly, that it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it, and that care of the soul matters more than wealth or reputation. He refused payment and, in Plato's account, accepted death (399 BC) rather than give up his philosophical mission. So the contrast is between objective moral truth and conventionalism, and between moral knowledge and skill in persuasion.

**Antithesis: the opposition is less than diametrical (6 marks).**

First, both turned philosophy from the study of the cosmos, which occupied the pre-Socratics, to human affairs: law, virtue, education and the city. Second, both used argument as their tool: question and answer, the testing of definitions and the exposure of contradictions. Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds (423 BC) presents Socrates as a Sophist, which shows that many Athenians did not tell them apart. Third, some Sophists did care about virtue and civic education (Protagoras claims in Plato's dialogue to teach good judgement in public affairs), and some argued from nature that all human beings are kin, a humane view that Socrates would not have rejected. Fourth, our picture of the Sophists comes largely from Plato and Aristotle, who were their critics, so part of the contrast may be polemical. Finally, Socrates himself never set out a finished doctrine of definitions or of the forms; that development belongs to Plato, so the strictness of the "Socratic" epistemology is itself debated.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** The opposition is real concerning foundations and aims: truth against appearance, virtue as knowledge against virtue as skill, a disinterested search against a paid profession. It is not real concerning subject matter and method, which they shared. Socrates can be seen as a thinker who arises from the sophistic enlightenment and turns its own critical tools against its relativist conclusions.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** The assertion is largely justified when ethics and epistemology are considered: Socrates defended objective moral and intellectual standards, the Sophists generally denied them. It becomes an exaggeration if "diametrically" is taken to mean that nothing was common to them, since they shared the human turn of philosophy and the use of argument. The better judgement is that Socrates was the Sophists' most radical critic from within their own intellectual world.
